newsitem.title: USA: Montgomery Ward gets $300 million cash infusion.
newsitem.headline: Montgomery Ward gets $300 million cash infusion.

text.p: Montgomery Ward & Co. got a $300 million cash infusion Tuesday to stay afloat during its bankruptcy reorganization, and the retailer said it had not determined how many stores or employees would be lost in the process.
The 408-store chain, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Monday, said in a court filing in Wilmington, Del., that it had "virtually no cash on hand."

It received approval from a U.S. bankruptcy judge for the $300 million financing from General Electric Co.'s GE Capital Services to buy new inventory and cover other costs. The financing is part of a $1 billion commitment from GE that has yet to be approved by the court.

"Chapter 11 gives Montgomery Ward the opportunity to reorganize and restructure," Chairman and Chief Executive Roger Goddu said in a statement. "At the moment, we have made no decision on additional store closings or layoffs."
Still, experts said Montgomery Ward needed to shut down many of its stores to pare losses. It lost $249 million last year on $6.6 billion in revenues.

The company told lenders last month that it would close 100 stores, including its Lechmere consumer electronics division, which it bought in 1994, according to an individual familiar with documents provided to Montgomery Ward's lenders.

Mongtomery Ward officials were not available to comment. The 125-year-old department store chain had been negotiating desperately with lenders on a financing package involving fresh funding to pay vendors and to obtain waivers on $1.4 billion in debt.
The talks collapsed after Montgomery Ward's lenders, including banks and insurance companies, balked at details of the rescue package put together by GE Capital.

Under the deal, the banks and insurance companies would have received $600 million from the sale of Montgomery Ward's direct-marketing unit Signature Group in exchange for waivers on the debt, a source said. But the lenders wanted GE Capital to guarantee the payment, which GE was not willing to do.
GE Capital officials were not available to comment.

Signature Group was not a part of the bankruptcy filing. In Delaware, Spencer Heine, executive vice president of Montgomery Ward, said the company was "still close" to reaching a deal to sell Signature to HFS Inc., a large hotel franchiser and owner of Avis car rental company.

Last week Ward said it would remodel four to six stores early next year to boost sales and attract more women shoppers. It defined its target customer as between 30 and 55 years old and earning $25,000 to $50,000 a year. The company said it would stock more attractive apparel and focus on its core appliance and furniture businesses.
Wall Street analysts, however, said the strategy would pit Montgomery Ward against more successful competitors such as Sears, Roebuck and Co., Kohl's Corp and J.C. Penney Co. Inc.
"Doing an apparel repositioning is a difficult and very competitive strategy," said Michael Exstein of CS First Boston.
